notes.b: The rate of a reaction is how fast reactants are used up or products appear. You can measure it over a whole stretch of time (average rate) or at the very start (initial rate), and the two give different answers.
points: Average rate over a time interval is the change in the amount of product or reactant divided by the time taken, for example the total volume of gas divided by the total time.
Initial rate is the rate at the very start (t = 0). It is the greatest rate of the whole reaction because the reactant concentrations are highest then.
The initial rate is the gradient (slope) of the tangent drawn to the curve at the origin. A tangent is a straight line that just touches a curve at one point without cutting it.
A clock reaction is one timed until a fixed amount of product forms, such as the sulfur cross, where you time how long until a mark is hidden. For these, 1/time measures the initial rate.
1/time works as the initial rate because in a clock reaction only a small fraction of the reactants has been used in the time taken, so the rate has hardly changed.
notes.tip: Initial rates come from a tangent at the origin, not from dividing a reading by its time, which only gives an average rate. Initial and average rates are for all students.

notes.h: Worked example: rates from a graph (sample data)
notes.b: Here one set of results is used to find an average rate, compare two minutes and find an initial rate. Follow the arithmetic step by step so you can repeat it on any graph or table.
points: Sample data: oxygen from hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. Time (min) and volume (cm³): 0, 0; 1, 21; 2, 36; 3, 47; 4, 56; 5, 62; 6, 67; 8, 73; 10, 76; 12, 78; 14, 79; 16, 80; 18, 80.
The reaction is complete when the volume stops changing. Here it levels at 80 cm³, at about 16 min.
Average rate over the first 4 min = 56 cm³ ÷ 4 min = 14.0 cm³ min⁻¹.
Average rate in the first minute = 21 cm³ min⁻¹.
Average rate in the second minute = (36 − 21) cm³ ÷ 1 min = 15 cm³ min⁻¹. This is lower than the first minute because the concentration of H₂O₂ has fallen as it is used up.
Initial rate: the tangent at the origin passes through (1.0 min, 24 cm³), so the initial rate = 24 cm³ ÷ 1.0 min = 24.0 cm³ min⁻¹.
To convert a rate in g min⁻¹ to mol min⁻¹, divide by the molar mass (the mass of one mole): M(CO₂) = 44 g mol⁻¹ (C 12, O 16).
If the mass of CO₂ lost is 0.220 g min⁻¹ (sample data), the rate = 0.220 g min⁻¹ ÷ 44 g mol⁻¹ = 5.00 × 10⁻³ mol CO₂ min⁻¹.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to plot volume or mass against time, read off volumes and times, find when the reaction ended, calculate an average rate over an interval, and compare the first and second minutes. They also ask you to convert a rate in g min⁻¹ to mol min⁻¹.

notes.b: The rate keeps changing as reactants are used up, so sometimes you need the rate at one exact moment. A tangent to the curve gives it.
points: Instantaneous rate is the rate at one particular moment: the gradient of the tangent drawn to the curve at that time.
To draw the tangent, place a ruler so that it touches the curve at the chosen time without cutting it, and draw a long straight line. A long line makes the gradient more accurate.
Pick two points far apart on the tangent line and calculate gradient = change in y ÷ change in x. Points far apart reduce the error in reading the graph.
The instantaneous rate falls during the reaction because the reactants are used up. The average rate over an interval lies between the instantaneous rates at its start and end.
Instantaneous rate at 2.0 min, from the sample data above: the tangent passes through (0 min, 10 cm³) and (5.0 min, 76 cm³), so the rate = (76 − 10) cm³ ÷ (5.0 − 0) min = 13.2 cm³ min⁻¹.
notes.tip: Instantaneous rate is Higher Level only. Find it from a tangent at the stated time, not by dividing a reading by its time, which gives an average rate.

notes.h: Investigation 1: calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid, surface area and concentration: method
notes.b: This reaction gives off carbon dioxide gas, so the mass of the flask falls as the reaction goes. Weighing the flask over time lets you follow the rate and test two factors: particle size and acid concentration.
points: Aim: to investigate the effect of particle size (and of acid concentration) on the rate of reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid.
Equation: CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).
1. Place a conical flask (a flask with a flat base and narrow neck) containing a known mass, e.g. 10 g, of large marble chips (calcium carbonate) on an electronic balance.
2. Put a graduated cylinder holding a known volume, e.g. 50 cm³, of 1.0 M hydrochloric acid beside the flask, and record the total mass.

notes.h: Investigation 1: running the reaction and varying the factor
notes.b: With the flask set up on the balance, you start the reaction and record the falling mass, then repeat with one factor changed.
points: 3. Pour in the acid, put a loose cotton-wool plug in the neck, and start the stopwatch at once.
4. Record the mass every 30 s for about 10 min, until it stops changing. The loss in mass is the mass of CO₂ given off.
5. Repeat with the same mass of small chips or powder, with the same volume and concentration of acid at the same temperature.
6. For concentration, repeat with the same size and mass of chips and the same volume of acid at different concentrations, e.g. 0.5 M, 1.0 M and 2.0 M. (M means mol L⁻¹.)
Alternative: collect the CO₂ in a gas syringe (a calibrated syringe that the gas pushes out) and record its volume every 30 s.
Diagram: conical flask with marble chips and acid, loose cotton-wool plug, on an electronic balance; a graduated cylinder of acid beside it; a stopwatch.

notes.b: Plotting the results shows which conditions give the faster reaction. Each choice in the method also has a reason, which is what makes the test fair.
points: Plot mass of CO₂ lost (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for each run on the same axes. The steeper initial curve shows the faster rate.
Smaller chips give a steeper curve, a faster rate, because of their greater surface area: more calcium carbonate is exposed to the acid at once.
More concentrated acid gives a faster rate. There is more on this in Rate of reaction and collision theory.
The chips are in excess (more than enough), so the acid is the limiting reactant (the one that runs out first and so sets the total amount of product).
Because the acid is the limiting reactant, more concentrated acid of the same volume also gives more CO₂ in total.
The cotton-wool plug lets CO₂ escape but stops acid spray being lost, which would otherwise add to the mass loss and give a false result.
The same mass of carbonate and the same acid keep the test fair, so only the factor you chose changes.
notes.tip: A changed-condition question wants the effect and its reason: small chips give a faster rate because of greater surface area. For acid concentration, say that the same volume of more concentrated acid also gives more CO₂ in total because the acid is the limiting reactant.

notes.h: Investigation 2: sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid, concentration and temperature: setting up
notes.b: In this reaction a solid forms and slowly turns the solution cloudy. Timing how long until a cross under the flask disappears gives a measure of rate without any gas collection.
points: Aim: to investigate the effect of concentration and of temperature on rate.
Equation: Na₂S₂O₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + SO₂(g) + S(s) + H₂O(l).
The pale yellow sulfur precipitate (an insoluble solid formed in a solution) makes the solution cloudy until it hides the cross.
Draw a dark cross on white paper and place a conical flask on it, so you can look down through the solution at the cross.
Look down through the solution from above and stop the watch when the cross can no longer be seen. Record the time.

notes.b: To change the concentration you dilute the thiosulfate with water. The total volume must stay the same so that the only thing that changes is the concentration.
points: Make a series of thiosulfate solutions of the same total volume, e.g. 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 cm³ of 0.20 M Na₂S₂O₃, each made up to 50 cm³ with deionised water (water with dissolved ions removed). This gives 0.20, 0.16, 0.12, 0.08 and 0.04 M.
Dilute with water only, using a burette or graduated pipette (accurate glass tubes for measuring liquid volumes), and keep the total volume constant.
Pour one solution into the flask, add a fixed volume of acid, e.g. 10 cm³ of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid, quickly, swirl, and start the stopwatch at the same moment.
Repeat for each concentration, keeping the acid volume and concentration, total volume, temperature, flask, cross and observer the same. Calculate rate = 1/time.
notes.tip: When diluting the thiosulfate, keep the total volume constant and add water, not acid. Start the stopwatch at the moment of mixing. You may be asked how to dilute the thiosulfate.

notes.b: To test temperature, the concentration is fixed and the starting temperature is changed with a water bath (a container of water held at a set temperature).
points: Use the same concentration each time, e.g. 0.05 M Na₂S₂O₃, so that temperature is the only factor that changes.
Warm the thiosulfate in a water bath to the chosen temperature, e.g. 20, 30, 40 or 50 °C, add the acid, start timing, and record the temperature of the mixture with a thermometer.
Use the average of the start and end temperatures, because the mixture does not stay at one temperature during the run.

notes.b: Converting each time into a rate (1/time) lets you plot rate against the factor and draw a conclusion. These results are sample data.
points: Sample data, concentration: 0.20 M, 20 s; 0.16 M, 25 s; 0.12 M, 34 s; 0.08 M, 50 s; 0.04 M, 102 s.
Rates (1/time) for those concentrations: 0.0500, 0.0400, 0.0294, 0.0200 and 0.0098 s⁻¹.
A graph of rate against concentration is a straight line through the origin, so rate is directly proportional to concentration.
Sample data, temperature: 20 °C, 80 s; 30 °C, 41 s; 40 °C, 21 s; 50 °C, 11 s.
Rates (1/time) for those temperatures: 0.0125, 0.0244, 0.0476 and 0.0909 s⁻¹.
A graph of rate against temperature is a curve rising ever more steeply. The rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise.
The same total volume means the same depth of liquid over the cross, so the same amount of sulfur hides it in each run.
1/time is used as the measure of rate because a shorter time means a faster rate.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why 1/time is a measure of rate, then plot rate against concentration or temperature and draw a conclusion.

notes.b: Sulfur dioxide is made in this reaction, so there is a safety point to state. The timing relies on judgement, so there are also errors to know.
points: Safety: sulfur dioxide is a toxic, choking gas that is dangerous for people with asthma. Work in a well-ventilated room, do not heat above about 60 °C, and pour the mixture away promptly when each run ends.
Judging when the cross disappears is subjective (it depends on the person looking), so use the same observer and the same cross.
A delay in starting the stopwatch affects the time recorded, because the clock must start the moment the solutions mix.
The temperature falls during a warm run, which is why the average of the start and end temperatures is used.
Diagram: conical flask standing on white paper marked with a cross, eye looking down from above; thermometer and water bath for the temperature runs.
notes.tip: Be ready to describe the thiosulfate cross experiment for concentration or temperature, and the safety point for sulfur dioxide.

notes.h: Investigation 3: decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, catalyst and concentration: method
notes.b: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly into water and oxygen. Manganese(IV) oxide speeds this up, and collecting the oxygen lets you follow the rate.
points: Aim: to measure the rate of decomposition (breaking down) of hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide catalyst (a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up), and to investigate the effect of one factor: the concentration of H₂O₂, the form of the catalyst, or the temperature.
Equation: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g).
1. Place a measured volume of dilute hydrogen peroxide, e.g. 5 cm³ of 20-volume H₂O₂ diluted to 25 cm³ with deionised water, in a conical flask.
20-volume hydrogen peroxide gives 20 cm³ of oxygen per cm³ of solution on complete decomposition.
2. Put a small mass, e.g. 0.5 g, of manganese(IV) oxide (manganese dioxide, MnO₂), a black powder, in a small test tube. Lower it into the flask on a thread so that it does not touch the peroxide.
3. Stopper the flask, with a delivery tube leading to an inverted graduated cylinder full of water in a basin, or to a gas syringe.
4. Tilt or shake the flask so the catalyst mixes with the peroxide, and start the stopwatch at the same instant. This starts the reaction without losing any oxygen.
5. Record the volume of oxygen every 30 s or 1 min until no more gas is produced; swirl the flask throughout.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to draw the apparatus for measuring oxygen from hydrogen peroxide, to say how to add the catalyst without losing gas, and to describe MnO₂ (a black powder).

notes.h: Investigation 3: varying the factor, control and safety
notes.b: Once the basic run works, you change one factor at a time and compare. A control and a safety check complete the investigation.
points: Repeat, changing one factor: e.g. half the concentration of H₂O₂ with the same total volume, or granules instead of powder with the same mass, keeping everything else the same.
A control (a run with the factor you are testing left out): hydrogen peroxide without catalyst gives almost no oxygen over the same time. This shows the catalyst is what speeds the reaction.
The catalyst can be filtered off, washed, dried and weighed at the end to show it is unchanged in mass.

Safety: hydrogen peroxide is an oxidising agent (it readily causes other substances to be oxidised) and, in concentrated form, is corrosive to skin and eyes (it damages them on contact). Wear goggles and gloves.
Store hydrogen peroxide in a cool, dark place, because it decomposes in light and heat, building up pressure.
Diagram: conical flask with H₂O₂ and a small test tube of MnO₂ hanging on a thread; stopper and delivery tube to an inverted graduated cylinder of water in a trough, or to a gas syringe.
notes.tip: Safety with hydrogen peroxide is examined: state the hazard (oxidising agent, corrosive in concentrated form), goggles and gloves, and cool dark storage.

notes.b: A graph of gas volume against time changes in predictable ways when you change a condition. The gradient shows the rate, and the final level shows how much product could form.
points: A faster rate gives a steeper initial curve that levels off sooner. The causes are a higher temperature, a catalyst, powder instead of lumps, or a more concentrated excess reactant.
A faster rate gives the same final volume if the amount of limiting reactant (the reactant that runs out first) is unchanged.
A slower rate, from a lower temperature (e.g. ice-water), larger lumps or no catalyst, gives a less steep curve that takes longer to level off.
A slower rate also gives the same final volume if the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged.
Halving the concentration of the limiting reactant, at the same volume, gives a less steep curve and half the final volume, because there is half as much reactant to form product.
The final volume of gas tells you the amount of limiting reactant; the gradient tells you the rate.

Secondary data (values you are given, not ones you measured) come from a graph or table, such as the volume at a stated time, the time to reach a volume, the time the reaction ended or half the final volume.
Use secondary data to calculate rates as above, and instantaneous rates at Higher Level.
notes.tip: A catalyst or temperature change does not change the final volume of gas; changing the amount of limiting reactant does. When sketching a curve for half concentration, powder or ice-water, justify it.

keyTerms.definition: The change in amount of product or reactant divided by the time taken over a stated interval.
The rate at the very start of a reaction (t = 0), given by the gradient of the tangent to the curve at the origin.
The rate at one particular moment, given by the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that time.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point without cutting it, used to find the gradient and so the rate at that point.
A reaction timed until a fixed amount of product forms, so that 1/time gives a measure of the initial rate.
A repeat of the experiment without the factor being tested, used to show that the factor causes the change observed.
Data taken from a given graph or table rather than measured in the experiment itself.
Water from which dissolved ions have been removed, used to dilute solutions without adding unwanted ions.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate the effect of concentration on the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid. Explain how the rate is found and what the graph of rate against concentration shows.
questions.model: Make a series of sodium thiosulfate solutions of the same total volume by diluting 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 cm³ of 0.20 M Na₂S₂O₃ each to 50 cm³ with deionised water, giving 0.20, 0.16, 0.12, 0.08 and 0.04 M. Draw a dark cross on white paper and place a conical flask on it. Pour one solution into the flask, add a fixed volume of 2.0 M hydrochloric acid, e.g. 10 cm³, quickly, swirl, and start the stopwatch at the same moment. Look down through the solution from above and stop the watch when the cross can no longer be seen. Keep the acid volume and concentration, total volume, temperature, flask, cross and observer the same for each run. The rate is 1/time, because a shorter time means a faster rate and the same amount of sulfur hides the cross each time. Plotting rate against concentration gives a straight line through the origin, showing that rate is directly proportional to concentration. Sample data: at 0.20 M the time is 20 s, a rate of 1/20 s = 0.0500 s⁻¹; at 0.04 M the time is 102 s, a rate of 1/102 s = 0.0098 s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: (Sample data) Hydrogen peroxide was decomposed with a catalyst. Time (min) and volume of O₂ (cm³): 0, 0; 1, 30; 2, 50; 3, 63; 4, 71; 5, 75. (i) Calculate the average rate over the first 3 minutes. (ii) Calculate the average rate during the second minute and explain why it differs from the rate in the first minute. (iii) (Higher Level) A tangent drawn at 2.0 min passes through (0 min, 17 cm³) and (4.0 min, 83 cm³). Calculate the instantaneous rate at 2.0 min.
questions.model: (i) Average rate = 63 cm³ ÷ 3 min = 21.0 cm³ min⁻¹. (ii) Rate in the second minute = (50 − 30) cm³ ÷ 1 min = 20 cm³ min⁻¹. This is lower than the 30 cm³ min⁻¹ in the first minute because the concentration of H₂O₂ has fallen as it is used up. (iii) Instantaneous rate = (83 − 17) cm³ ÷ (4.0 − 0) min = 66 ÷ 4.0 = 16.5 cm³ min⁻¹.

questions.prompt: On a graph of volume of oxygen against time, sketch and explain the curves you would expect if the experiment were repeated (i) with the flask in ice-water, (ii) with the same volume of hydrogen peroxide of half the concentration.
questions.model: (i) In ice-water the rate is lower: the particles have less kinetic energy, so fewer collisions have energy at or above the activation energy. The curve is less steep at the start and takes longer to level off, but it reaches the same final volume, because the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged. (ii) Half the concentration gives a less steep curve, because there are fewer particles per unit volume and fewer collisions per second. The final volume is half as large, because there is half as much hydrogen peroxide to form oxygen.
